tasks.progress: FINAL STATE (D148/D149): a tuned MoE configuration EXISTS and is IN PRODUCTION - the prefill MoE tiles are part of the selected running preset at <tuning>/moe_configs. Read the entries below as the chronological path, not the conclusion: the decode-side autotuner failed (D144), then the route was reopened with a search targeting real prefill batches and succeeded. · D143 addendum 2: MoE autotune ATTEMPTED and INCOMPLETE - no tuned config produced, no A/B run, G6 unaffected. Five blockers found and fixed: (1) benchmark_moe.py hard-imports ray -> installed ray 2.58.0 (protobuf UNCHANGED at 6.33.6; only msgpack+ray added); (2) ray died on libamd_smi.so - the lib is present but its DEP DIR /opt/rocm/core-7.14/lib/rocm_sysdeps/lib was not on the loader path (this also means the amdsmi sitecustomize shim has been SILENTLY failing all along); (3) AttributeError num_local_experts -> patched with num_experts fallback; (4) would have written N=5632 (the DENSE intermediate_size) instead of N=640 (moe_intermediate_size) -> patched, caught by the filename pre-check; (5) ray rejects ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES while benchmark_moe.py itself swaps HIP->ROCR unconditionally (written for old Ray) -> patched to gate on ray version. SIXTH BLOCKER UNRESOLVED: ray workers SEGFAULT importing torch inside the benchmark actor. Not OOM (cgroup oom_kill 0, 127 GB free) and not a general ray/torch incompatibility (isolation probe: ray fine, torch fine in a worker, num_gpus=1 pinning fine). Wanted file: E=128,N=640,device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics,dtype=int4_w4a16.json (vLLM ships 332 configs, all NVIDIA). RECOMMENDATION: write a minimal ray-free tuner - everything needed is now known. Serve untouched; rig idle. · TITLE CORRECTED (D144 bookkeeping): O4 previously read 'lm_head int8 shadow', but the task has been carrying MoE autotune. The lm_head int8 idea is NOT lost - it belongs with the dense/GEMV work (D143 ranks gemm_dense as the highest-headroom code target). · D144: the ray-free tuner (tools/m0/moe_tune_noray.py) WORKS - it reused upstream's real tune()/benchmark_config via ActorClass.__ray_metadata__.modified_class, forced the known shape (E=128, shard_intermediate=1280, hidden=2560, topk=10, group=128, int4_w4a16), and produced exactly E=128,N=640,device_name=AMD_Radeon_Graphics,dtype=int4_w4a16.json. The serve demonstrably LOADED it (fused_moe.py:1154). A/B/A' result: controls agreed to 0.05% (47.63 vs 47.65 tok/s) and the tuned arm was 24.94 tok/s = -47.7%, with ALL 9 artifacts byte-identical (sha 0128852903291e32) so it is numerics-safe but a pure perf regression. REJECTED - do not use VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER. The upstream autotuner's objective does not transfer to this stack. Also caught a regression: merely INSTALLING ray broke the serve (vLLM imports ray at startup and ray's AMD guard rejects ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES); ray+msgpack were uninstalled and the serve re-verified. PIVOT per plan: dense GEMV geometry (D143's highest-headroom/lowest-risk target). topkGating 449 ms was never in scope here. · CORRECTION BY THE EXPERT REVIEW (D148), which supersedes the 'closed as a dead end' framing for the PREFILL path: the old tuner bypassed its candidate settings for small batches and let its largest small-batch entry control much larger prefills, so D144 was measuring the wrong workload with the wrong search. The replacement search targets ACTUAL prefill batches and preserves small-batch defaults; all 68 initial and 65 extended cases passed their numerical comparisons, and the MoE-only full-model arm matched all nine control prompt cases exactly across all 27 scored outputs. Selected file uses M/N/K tiles of 8/64/32 at batch 128/256/512, 32/64/32 at 1,024, and 32/64/32 with one stage at 1,536/2,048; isolated in its own tuning folder; no compiled extension rebuilt and every original binary hash still matches. D144's decode-side finding stands: a config tuned for one shape does not transfer to another.

tasks.progress: FINAL STATE: closed with NO code change. The lever was measured down rather than abandoned blindly - lm_head is at 96% of the HBM ceiling and the family's realistic ceiling is ~2.6% of wall, which the expert review independently corroborated (its production-compatible wave64 sweep found only modest shape-dependent gains and selected no C++ geometry change). Read on for the measurements. · NEXT TARGET (D143 profile, reaffirmed by D144). gemm_dense is 24.3% of TP4 kernel time - the largest single family - and gemv_f16_rdna2_<8,1> alone accounts for 1253 ms across 50,691 launches (~24.7 us each). That is ~24x lower arithmetic intensity than a tuned GEMM, so geometry/tile selection is the lever. D143 ranks this the highest-headroom AND lowest-risk code target, ahead of MoE. Scope note: the old O4 title mentioned an 'lm_head int8 shadow' - lm_head GEMV is part of this family, so that idea lives here now. Method: freeze the current serve config (TP4 MTP=0 fp16 graphs-no-compile, AR on, no offload, VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER deliberately UNSET per D144), change ONE thing, and gate with A/B/A' because whole-serve drift is ~1%. REJECTED: WAVES sweep (-5.1% total, and mechanistically cannot help - grid*block gives total threads ~= N*32 regardless of WAVES, so it never changes occupancy). FALSIFIED OWN HYPOTHESIS: I claimed the k-loop was un-unrolled; it is already a 4-deep predicated unroll using __builtin_amdgcn_fdot2. My variant was based on a partial file read and silently produced zeros; only the U=1 control (which must reproduce production) caught it. RESIZED: gemv_f16_rdna2 is 15.2% of kernel time, and the whole lever's realistic ceiling is ~2.6% of WALL, with lm_head contributing 0%; each sub-lever is 0.4-1.6%, at/below the ~1% noise floor. NEXT: either implement split-K for the small-N family (~0.6% expected, likely rejected) or RE-TARGET to elementwise (11.8% of kernel time, 303,380 launches, launch-count-dominated - a different failure mode with more upside). · D145 addendum (attribution pass): the requested >80% kernel->op linkage is NOT achievable from this trace - measured 13.1% over 317,447 family launches. Cause is structural: a kernel's External id equals the launching event's Ev Idx, but cuda_runtime events carry NO Ev Idx (221,038 runtime vs 162,245 cpu_ops), so most kernels point at an un-indexable event; correlation->flow-start cannot rescue it either (only 15,757 's' events vs 221,038 'f'). Containment must use the launching CPU thread - GPU kernels are on stream tids, so same-tid containment scores 0%. A better trace is needed for op-level attribution; the BY-NAME ranking needs no ids and is complete: family = 12.56% of kernel time. Arithmetic gate: >=2.3% of kernel time is needed for a 2% wall win, and the largest single name (copyBuffer) is 1.76%, so the unit must be a count-clustered GROUP. Candidates: copyish family 4.26% kernel = ~3.65% wall (the only group above the bar); a 5x ~13,716 cluster (MeanOps+pow+rsqrt+float16_copy+direct_copy) = one eager RMSNorm decomposition ~3.0% kernel ~2.5% wall, BUT it contradicts D118-D121 ('norms already fused') and must be reconciled first; ~27,431x2 (fp16->fp32 copy + OnSelf_add<float>) ~1.7% wall; ~25,650x2 (Fill<Half> + add<Half>) ~1.6% wall. NEXT (operator-approved pivot): a DIRECT causAL test - toggle VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM in an A/B/A' to test whether the ~47.5k copyBuffer launches are the per-call `.contiguous()` at utils.py:289. Split-K deliberately SKIPPED (~0.6% wall, eaten by the reduction launch). · D146 CLOSED: skinny-GEMM causal test. (1) The copyBuffer hypothesis is REFUTED - toggling VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM leaves EVERY elementwise family byte-identical (copyBuffer 12,295 in all three arms; fp16->fp32 7,128; fill 7,580; mul 9,752 etc.) while total kernel time differed 2.3x (3755 vs 8594 ms), so the copies are genuinely orthogonal to the GEMM path. The `x.reshape(-1,k).contiguous()` at utils.py:289 is NOT the source; copy attribution is CLOSED per operator rule. (2) VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM is worth 2.83x - ON 47.51 tok/s vs OFF 16.76, with controls agreeing to 0.02% (47.51 vs 47.52, the tightest A/B/A' yet) and all 9 gates deterministic. tasks.title: TP8 go/no-go - CAPACITY decision only: TP8 is a cheap-capacity strategy, NOT a performance strategy (D151)
tasks.acceptance: All 56 ordered pairs byte-exact at ~14 GB/s AND small-message all-reduce latency at world=8 still in the tens of microseconds; otherwise stop
tasks.progress: FINAL VERDICT (D151, operator conclusion) - read this before acting on the D150 recommendation. **TP8 is a cheap-capacity strategy, not a performance strategy.** It may let the rig run models or context sizes that are otherwise uneconomical, but it should NOT be expected to deliver better decode throughput than the current TP4 setup. REALISTIC EXPECTATION: TP8 decode will probably land BELOW the current ~40-60 tok/s aggregate range - unless the 8-GPU machine has a MUCH better interconnect/topology than this one. USE-CASE OUTLOOK: single-stream decode likely WORSE than TP4; multi-user decode throughput likely FLAT to worse; long prefill/TTFT maybe acceptable, possibly modestly better; capacity per dollar is STILL THE MAIN REASON to do TP8; the overall 'cheap 128 GB serving box' is viable only if speed expectations are modest. FOUR SIGNALS: aggregate decode stays ~40-45 tok/s from 1 to 8 concurrency (more requests do not fill unused compute); per-request speed collapses as concurrency rises (requests share the same bottleneck); GPU power DROPS to ~111 W at 4-8 concurrency (the GPUs are waiting more, not working harder); p95 rises sharply (scheduler/communication bubbles become user-visible). If this were compute-limited, aggregate would CLIMB with concurrency and power would stay near 150 W - instead aggregate is flat and power falls, pointing to synchronization, communication, scheduler overhead or CPU/NUMA stalls rather than a lack of active requests. THE POWER DROP IS DECISIVE: at 4-way concurrency there should have been plenty of queued work, yet the rig backed off to ~111 W - a saturated machine cannot reduce its draw when handed MORE work. AND ADDING RANKS IS UNLIKELY TO FIX IT: four more TP ranks usually INCREASE collective cost and synchronization pressure, so TP8 pushes the wrong way on the exact axis that already limits the rig. The one escape hatch is a materially better interconnect/topology than the PEX88096 one measured here - which is what the physical pre-checks establish. SO: the checks remain worth doing but justified by CAPACITY PER DOLLAR, not by any decode-speed expectation. If the goal is decode throughput, the lever is the per-token serialized work identified in D145/D146 and confirmed here - not more cards.

tasks.title: TP8 probe - decode concurrency sweep: aggregate FLAT 1->8, refutes the weight-bandwidth case (D150)
tasks.acceptance: Aggregate and per-request throughput, round latency median/p95, and GPU power measured at 1/2/4/8 concurrent decode-heavy requests
tasks.progress: DONE (D150 addendum). 1K prompt, 512 generated, greedy, STREAMING (so round latency is measured, not inferred), unique prompt salt per request, GPU sampled at 1 Hz per phase. RESULTS: aggregate 44.41 / 40.21 / 45.24 / 40.30 tok/s at concurrency 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 = FLAT (12% band, no trend); scaling 1.00x / 0.91x / 1.02x / 0.91x. Ideal linear scaling at 4 would be 178 tok/s, measured 45 = NONE. Per-request 52.39 / 25.37 / 13.62 / 11.37 tok/s (scales ~1/n as expected). Round median 43.2 / 66.0 / 197.2 / 200.6 ms and p95 143.6 / 174.8 / 308.0 / 348.5 ms with multi-second stalls (3466 ms max at 2), so interactive feel degrades under load. GPU POWER FALLS as concurrency rises - 150.0 / 146.5 / 111.0 / 109.0 W - while the use counter stays ~100%, i.e. the SMs are STALLED WAITING, not saturated: the workload is LATENCY/SERIALIZATION BOUND and the 100% use figure counts issue cycles, not useful work. THIS REFUTES the weight-bandwidth case for TP8 (see D150 section 6): if weights bound decode, batching 4 would read them once and emit 4x the tokens; it emitted 1.0x. So the earlier 18.23 GiB / 810 GB/s ~= 44 tok/s agreement with the measured ~47.7 was a NUMERICAL COINCIDENCE - the MoE is sparse (top-10 of 128 local experts) so the full per-rank footprint is never read per token. CONSISTENT WITH D145/D146: the elementwise/copy residue is 303k latency-bound launches. Measurement trap hit and fixed: the first pass counted streamed CHUNKS as tokens, understating throughput ~2.8x because MTP2 puts several accepted tokens in one chunk; usage.completion_tokens is authoritative and the ratios were unaffected. · CONSEQUENCE (D151): this sweep is the evidence base for the final verdict that TP8 is a cheap-capacity strategy, not a performance strategy - aggregate decode flat from 1 to 8 concurrency, GPU power FALLING to ~111 W while 'use' stays 100%, and sharply rising p95. Expect TP8 decode to land BELOW the current ~40-60 tok/s aggregate range unless the 8-GPU machine has a much better interconnect. Do not treat these numbers as a baseline that TP8 is expected to beat.

**Elementwise/copyBuffer attribution: the trace cannot resolve parents; the by-name ranking is complete (D145 addendum).** The requested >80% kernel->op linkage is unreachable - measured 13.1% over 317,447 family launches, because a kernel's External id points at the launching event's Ev Idx while cuda_runtime events carry no Ev Idx at all. Op-level attribution needs a better trace, not more analysis. The by-name data is unaffected and decides the ranking: the family is 12.56% of kernel time, but **a target must be >=2.3% of kernel time to clear the 2% wall bar and the largest single kernel is 1.76%** - so the unit of work is a count-clustered group. Only the copyish family clears it as a whole (4.26% kernel = ~3.65% wall). Next step is a direct causal test (toggle VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM) rather than more trace archaeology.

**Skinny-GEMM causal test: copyBuffer hypothesis REFUTED; skinny GEMM worth 2.83x (D146).** Toggling VLLM_ROCM_USE_SKINNY_GEMM left every elementwise family byte-identical (copyBuffer 12,295 launches in all three arms) while total kernel time differed 2.3x - so the copies are causally orthogonal to the dense-GEMM path and `utils.py:289`'s per-call `.contiguous()` is NOT their source. Copy attribution is CLOSED. Separately and confirmatorily: **skinny GEMM is worth 2.83x** (47.51 tok/s ON vs 16.76 OFF), with controls agreeing to 0.02% - the tightest A/B/A' yet - so the baseline config stands unchanged. Per operator direction the next target is **O5 / MTP=3** (documented 1.9x on V620); topkGating stays a harder post-MTP target.

**O5 MTP=3: LOSSLESS but NOT the 1.9x - REJECTED (D147).** MTP=3 reproduces the MTP=0 greedy output hash BYTE-IDENTICALLY, so the port's MTP integration is correct and the MTP=4 text-changing failure does not reproduce at 3 - a genuine new confirmation. But the performance does not transfer: best case ~+5% TG, worst case -5%, versus the 1.9x that made O5 attractive (the V620's 2.7-3.1 accepted tokens/step clearly does not hold on gfx906, as PORT-MAP warned). **Nothing adopted: the two metrics disagree in SIGN** (TG +5.2% vs gate -5.0%) and MTP=3's gate spread blew up to 11.3 vs the control's 0.5, while its prefill cost (-12%) and startup cost (72->83 s) are unambiguous. Operator targets MISSED: TG128 ~53-56 vs >75, PP ~350 vs >500. Phase 5 now has every candidate closed by evidence; the standing baseline remains ~47.7 tok/s (G6 gap ~4.6%). The diagnostic that would explain the shortfall is a direct acceptance-rate measurement (tools/rdna2/watch.py).

**OPTIMISATION CLOSED - final state selected by the operator (D148/D149).** <container> is running TP4+EP at 150 W/card with **MTP2**, tuned prefill MoE tiles, a mask-aware MI50 top-10 router, 2048-token prefill chunks and a **32768-token context**; TunableOp and dense INT8 are off. Three-run medians (exact prompt lengths, two warmups each, 128 generated tokens, zero cached prompt tokens): **1K - PP 641.9 tok/s, decode 60.34 · 10K - PP 806.9, decode 61.22 (range 39.02-65.35) · 30K - PP 805.1, decode 57.34.** Against the pre-review reference this is a **~45-75% prefill improvement at 128-1536 tokens** with a modest decode gain. **Two of my own conclusions were corrected by the review and are recorded as such:** (1) D144 closed MoE tuning as a dead end, but the route WORKS for prefill - the old tuner bypassed small-batch settings and let a small-batch entry govern much larger prefills, so it was measuring the wrong workload; the corrected search passed all 133 cases and matched all nine control prompts across 27 outputs. (2) More importantly, **the ~47.7 tok/s gate I had been using timed the whole HTTP request, so it includes prompt time and is not comparable to a decode rate** - the corrected reference is ~55-56 decode tok/s. Also dispositioned in the review: NUMA affinity flat; default all-reduce block policy won; GEMV/INT8 found only modest shape-dependent gains and NO C++ geometry change was selected (consistent with D145); elementwise/fill kernels were NOT removed speculatively because several initialise graph padding and state. Remaining MTP3-vs-MTP2 note: K=3 was tested here and rejected (A/B/A' metrics disagreed in sign); K=2 is what was selected.

**TP8 feasibility probe: viable, and the case is WEIGHT BANDWIDTH not collectives (D150).** Three captures done. (1) TOPOLOGY: all four MI50s hang off ONE PEX88096 under ONE root complex and ONE NUMA node, with every GPU pair uniform (weight 40, 2 hops, PCIE) - and the switch has SPARE downstream ports, including a whole second PEX88096 with nothing behind it, so four more cards can be added without crossing root complexes or NUMA nodes. This also CORRECTS D078: the links are Gen4 x16 (16.0GT/s), not Gen3. (2) RCCL at world=4 is strong at both ends: small-message all-reduce latency 24.6-30.8 us and FLAT, large messages saturating at 14.19 GB/s algbw - exactly the fabric's measured per-pair capability, with no degradation to 256 MiB. So the interconnect does not block TP8. Watch item: a hard algorithm knee at 32 KiB, with the workload's ~20 KB AR message sitting just below it. (3) A fresh TP4 baseline reproduces prefill faithfully (647/809/808) with decode 0.7-3.9% lower (59.9/58.9/55.1); 1 Hz monitoring shows the rig is POWER-CAP limited at ~148 W against the 150 W cap (sclk full only 12-21% of the time), not thermally throttled - though GPU1 runs 14-18 C hotter than GPU3, and the slowest rank gates every step. **Per the operator's rule the fresh run is now the TP8 reference.** The economics: TP4 decode is weight-bandwidth-bound (18.23 GiB/rank / ~810 GB/s ~= 44 tok/s, matching the measured ~47.7), so TP8's ~9.1 GiB/rank implies a ~89 tok/s CEILING - far more than anything the collectives will cost. Next gate is physical: 56-pair fabric matrix and world=8 RCCL before any software investment.

**Decode concurrency sweep: aggregate throughput is FLAT 1->8, and it REFUTES the weight-bandwidth case for TP8 (D150 addendum).** With 1K prompts and 512 generated tokens at 1/2/4/8 concurrent requests, aggregate throughput measured **44.4 / 40.2 / 45.2 / 40.3 tok/s** - flat within a 12% band, i.e. **1.0x scaling where ideal would be 4x**. Per-request falls ~1/n as expected (52.4 -> 11.4 tok/s), round p95 degrades 144 -> 348 ms with multi-second stalls. The decisive evidence is the POWER: **150.0 / 146.5 / 111.0 / 109.0 W** while the GPU use counter stays ~100%, so the SMs are **stalled waiting, not saturated** - the workload is latency/serialization bound. **This falsifies my own D150 projection:** if weights bound decode, batching 4 would read them once and emit 4x the tokens; it emitted 1.0x, so the earlier 18.23 GiB / 810 GB/s ~= 44 tok/s agreement with ~47.7 was a numerical coincidence (the MoE is sparse, so the full per-rank footprint is never read per token). **Revised verdict: TP8 will not improve decode throughput, single-stream or multi-stream; its case is CAPACITY** (far more than 32K context, or unquantized weights). TP8-4 is retargeted accordingly, and the physical pre-checks (56-pair matrix, world=8 RCCL) still stand. Consistent with D145/D146: the elementwise/copy residue is 303k latency-bound launches.

**FINAL TP8 VERDICT: a cheap-capacity strategy, not a performance strategy (D151).** **TP8 is expected to land BELOW the current ~40-60 tok/s aggregate decode range** unless the 8-GPU machine has a much better interconnect/topology than this one. Single-stream decode likely worse than TP4; multi-user decode throughput likely flat to worse; long prefill/TTFT maybe acceptable, possibly modestly better; **capacity per dollar remains the only strong reason to do TP8**, and the 'cheap 128 GB serving box' is viable only with modest speed expectations. The decisive evidence is the part that is hardest to argue with: **GPU power DROPPED to ~111 W at 4-way concurrency while the use counter stayed at 100%** - a saturated machine cannot reduce its draw when handed MORE work. Aggregate throughput was flat from 1 to 8 concurrency (ideal 4x, measured 1.0x), per-request speed collapsed, and p95 climbed 144 -> 348 ms. That points to synchronization, communication, scheduler overhead or CPU/NUMA stalls rather than a lack of active requests - and adding four more TP ranks would INCREASE collective cost and sync pressure, pushing the wrong way on the exact axis that already limits the rig. **If the goal is decode throughput, the lever is the per-token serialized work identified in D145/D146 - not more cards.** The physical pre-checks (56-pair fabric matrix, world=8 RCCL) remain worth doing but are now justified by capacity per dollar. The operating configuration is unchanged: MTP2 / 32K / 150 W with the D148/D149 presets.
